title: One Ruler: A Same-Hands Re-Evaluation of Bivariate Causal Direction on Tuebingen, with a Parameter-Free Compression Baseline
summary: Headline accuracies on the 102 Tübingen cause-effect pairs are compared across papers even though each number is produced under its authors' own protocol (different pair subsets, weightings, model selection and abstention), so the paper re-runs every competitor itself under one strict rule: no tuning, decision forced on every pair, official weights. As a clean reference point it introduces a zero-parameter baseline that quantizes both variables to 256 levels, sorts one by the other, first-differences to int8 and uses bz2 compressed length with a marginal normalization as the causal-direction score. Under this common ruler the baseline reaches 74.7% weighted accuracy on 102 pairs and 76.0% on the 100 pairs SLOPE uses (vs. 77.2% forced-decision SLOPE, McNemar p = 0.39), while the published 82.4% and 77.5% headlines are shown to be a decided-subset score and a mis-attribution respectively.

claims.statement: The parameter-free sorted-conditional bz2 compression baseline scores 74.7% weighted accuracy on the 102-pair Tübingen CEP set under forced decision with pre-registered settings and no tuning.
claims.split: all 102 eligible pairs, weighted by official pairmeta.txt weights
claims.table_ref: §4.1 and Abstract headline; Table 2, row 'Compression (ours, our 102 pairs)'

claims.reported_spread: bootstrap 95% CI [63.2, 84.7]% (n=1000); 200x split-half out-of-sample 74.8%; p = 3.7e-7 vs chance
claims.est_compute: CPU, ~0.2 s total for 102 pairs (1.0 ms/pair median, pure-Python bz2)

match_target.why: C1 is the paper's pre-registered headline and the cheapest possible reproduction: it needs only the public 102 Tübingen pairs, pairmeta.txt weights and one pure-Python bz2 scorer with no fitted parameters and no randomness — about 0.2 s of CPU, no SLOPE R code, no regression training — yet it is exactly the central claim (a zero-parameter compressor reaches the low-to-mid 70s under the strict common ruler). The competitor numbers in Table 2 are only interpretable relative to this number.

tolerance.why: Rule 3: weighted accuracy is a bounded accuracy-like score on a 102-pair set (far below 2,000 examples) and the paper prints it as a percentage. Rule 1 does not apply (only a bootstrap CI and a split-half estimate are given, not a std over repeated runs), and rule 2 fails the 2,000-example threshold. Band is therefore 2.0 absolute percentage points — 72.7–76.7% — which also comfortably contains the reported bootstrap CI endpoints' neighbourhood and the 76.0% same-subset figure.

requirements.stmt: Restrict to the 102 CEP pairs that have a scalar cause, a scalar effect and at least 50 samples; drop multi-dimensional and short pairs.
requirements.quote: The 102 CEP pairs with scalar cause, scalar effect, and ≥50 samples, weighted by the official pairmeta.txt weights.

requirements.stmt: Force a decision on every pair (no abstention, no decision-rate curve, no top-k reporting); exact ties count as wrong.
requirements.quote: Every pair receives a {X →Y, Y →X} call; ties count as wrong. No abstention, no decision-rate curve, no top-k reporting.

requirements.stmt: Quantize each variable independently to 256 integer levels by linear min-max scaling (not standardization, not rank transform).
requirements.quote: quantize each independently to 256 levels by linear min-max scaling, giving integer sequences qx, qy ∈{0, . . . , 255}n

requirements.stmt: Define the sorted-conditional code as the bz2 byte length of the int8 first difference of the value sequence sorted by a stable argsort of the key sequence.
requirements.quote: where argsort is a stable sort, ∆the first difference cast to int8, and | · | the compressed byte length.

requirements.stmt: Normalize the conditional code by the marginal code dc(q)=|bz2(∆(q))| before differencing, using max(dc,1) as denominator.
Decide by the a-priori sign rule s>0 => X->Y and s<0 => Y->X, with |s| used only as confidence, never for tuning.
requirements.quote: the rule is a-priori: s > 0 ⇒X →Y , s < 0 ⇒Y →X, confidence |s|

requirements.stmt: Use the frozen settings: bz2 compression level 9, 256 levels, and linear subsampling of any series longer than 8000 points down to 8000 points.
requirements.cite: §3, 'Settings were frozen before any benchmark run'
requirements.quote: Settings were frozen before any benchmark run: bz2 level 9; 256 levels; series > 8000 points linearly subsampled to 8000.

requirements.stmt: Use bz2 as the compressor; lzma must not be substituted, because its container overhead makes both directions tie by construction at typical CEP lengths.
requirements.quote: bz2 (not lzma) is required: lzma’s container overhead makes output length-determined below ∼500 bytes, so both directions tie by construction on typical CEP series lengths

requirements.stmt: Keep the scorer parameter-free and untuned: no hyperparameter or model class may be chosen using benchmark accuracy.
requirements.quote: No hyperparameter or model class is selected using benchmark accuracy.

requirements.stmt: Do not standardize or rank-normalize the inputs; the input scaling must remain plain min-max on the raw values.
Report the headline as weighted accuracy over all 102 pairs, and also report the raw unweighted count (68/102) so weighted and unweighted numbers are not confused.
requirements.quote: By raw pair count the baseline is right on 68/102 (66.7% unweighted; the 74.7% headline is weighted).

requirements.stmt: Keep the whole decision path deterministic (no RNG, no seeds needed for the point estimate); randomness appears only in the diagnostic bootstrap/split-half checks.
requirements.quote: The headline result reproduces bit-for-bit (102/102 pairs agree on re-run).

data.name: Tübingen cause-effect pairs (CEP) with pairmeta.txt weights
data.how_to_get: Download the Mooij et al. [1] benchmark (pairmeta.txt, desc.txt, pair####.txt) from the Tübingen cause-effect page https://webdav.tuebingen.mpg.de/cause-effect/ ; keep pairs with scalar cause, scalar effect and >=50 samples (102 pairs) and use the official weights.

data.name: SLOPE released code and bundled CEP outputs (slope-v20181208, slope.tab, sloper.tab)
data.how_to_get: Marx & Vreeken SLOPE distribution (ICDM 2017, ref [6]); the paper obtained the authors' own R code and bundled outputs and re-releases its scoring harness at stateoftheart.nl/causal. Needed only for the competitor rows and for identifying the bundled 100-pair subset.

data.name: Mooij synthetic suites SIM, SIM-G, SIM-ln (100 pairs each)
data.how_to_get: Distributed with the Mooij et al. benchmark [1] and bundled in the SLOPE distribution; used only for the Table 3 generalization rows, not for the headline.

code_links: https://stateoftheart.nl/causal (stated in the paper: scorer, RECI re-implementation, SLOPE harness, per-pair outputs, bootstrap/split-half scripts, pre-registrations)
stated_compute: No hardware named — only 'the same machine' for timing: 'the median per-pair wall clock is 1.0 ms for ours (pure-Python bz2) vs. 24.4 ms for the authors’ SLOPE (≈24×); aggregate 0.20 s vs. 4.1 s.'
